doc.title: Laurence Juber interviewed by Monk Rowe, Glasgow, Scotland, July 27, 2016 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Altered tunings, Dan Foliart and Henry Worrall's Spanish Fandango
summary: Juber describes notation for altered tunings with Dan Foliart and the history from Worrall to open G tuning and 'Honky Tonk Woman'.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Well that particular composer, Dan Foliart, who I’ve worked with for over 30 years, he did “Roseanne,” “Home Improvement,” a lot of shows. We did a show for 11 years called “Seventh Heaven” where the acoustic guitar was extremely prominent. Finger style acoustic guitar. And he was always write in different tunings. But he knows the instrument. But how do you notate that? You can’t write tablature because the copyists wouldn’t know what to do with it. So we worked out a system where he would write it in standard notation and I would play it as though it were in standard tuning. So if I saw an E at the top of the stave, I would play the open top string, even though that might have been tuned to a D or a C sharp. So I had to turn off that inner ear thing that goes along with sight reading. And he would use multiple tunings during the session. So I’d have like two, three, sometimes even four guitars. And that kind of thing — we thought we’d invented that. And then I discovered that in fact in the mid-nineteenth century there was a man named Henry Worrall, who was a teacher at a girls’ school in Ohio, who published a piece called “The Spanish Fandango,” which was neither Spanish nor a fandango, but anything Spanish was extremely commercial at that point. And that was written in open G tuning. D-G-D-G-B-D. And he had actually published the same piece of music with a different set of variations a few years earlier under the name of “The Celebrated Violet Waltz.” And in that he used the normal practice, if you just write it the way it sounds, and you have to figure it out. I mean I’ve encountered pieces from the 1840s in open E tuning where you just have to do the transpositions. They don’t give you any hints. But what he did was Henry Worrall wrote out this piece so that you played it as though it were in standard tuning. You tune the guitar the way he says and then you play it like you read it in standard tuning. But what you hear is different. And so it actually had a little history. That piece has some very — the expression of that was very deep. Because it became, and some people will argue that it’s the root of the blues. It’s not. But the mechanics of tuning the guitar to an open chord really got established through that. Because that piece ended up in a lot of guitar tutor books, especially, there was a man named Septimus © Fillius Jazz Archive -16-

Winner who published The Eureka Method. And if you bought a guitar from Montgomery Ward or Sears, you would get this Eureka Method that would come with it. And so a lot of people learned how to play an open G tuning and you only need one finger to make chords. And you can play primary chords, open string, fifth fret, seventh fret. So yeah, I mean somebody that’s heading in the direction of a 12-bar blues will use that. And you can play — one of the things I do in my presentation is play the “Spanish Fandango” and then play the Rolling Stones’ “Honky Tonk Woman,” which was written in open G tuning. And the melody is almost identical in the chorus.
